Pims says its CT machine 'remains functional' following reports of failure to conduct Imran's heart scan. ISLAMABAD: Following reports that jailed PTI founder Imran Khan could not undergo a heart scan during a visit to the hospital last week, the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) said on Tuesday that its CT machine “remains functional and continues to support diagnostic services”. When Imran was brought to Pims last week for an eye procedure and other diagnostic examinations, doctors recommended a CT coronary angiography (CTA), but hospital staff reportedly said the facility was unavailable. After undergoing other tests, he was subsequently shifted back to Adiala Jail without the CTA, which can help detect coronary blockages and assess the risk of a heart attack. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also took notice of the non-functional CTA facility at Pims and constituted an inquiry committee to determine the facts. Sources had earlier told Dawn that the Cardiac Centre’s conventional angiography facility at Pims was different from a CTA. While conventional angiography involved inserting a catheter into a blood vessel, a CTA was performed using a CT scanner. In the statement issued on Tuesday, the Pims administration said, “[The] CT machine, installed in 2022, remains functional and continues to support diagnostic services.” It said that “imaging investigations are undertaken regularly on the basis of clinical assessment, specialist advice, patient-safety considerations and prescribed medical protocols”. “The use of a particular imaging procedure should be viewed within its clinical context and should not be interpreted unnecessarily,” it said. A senior doctor at Pims, who wished not to be named, told Dawn that around a dozen CTAs had been conducted before the statement was released. After reports regarding the failure to conduct the test had emerged, the PTI had reiterated its demand to move Imran to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad without any delay — which the Supreme Court had also directed on August 18. PTI Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram also cited details submitted to the court, saying a medical board constituted by the government had examined Imran on August 10 while a Pims cardiologist had already recommended the test for him on August 1 due to fluctuating blood pressure, palpitations, headaches, restlessness and the potential risk of cardiac complications arising from his age and prolonged isolation. “Even the government’s own doctors considered this diagnostic test necessary,” he said. “Yet, when Imran was taken to Pims, the procedure was not performed. Hospital officials claimed that the required facility was unavailable, despite the presence of a functional CT scanner in the radiology department capable of conducting the test,” he alleged.

Ayaz Sadiq says there is 'realisation' in govt about NA's lack of quorum, hopeful situation will improve. National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq on Tuesday said there was “realisation” among the treasury members about the lack of quorum in the House and he was hopeful that the situation would improve. Lately, NA proceedings have been marred by a lack of attendance amid a rift between the ruling PML-N and its main ally in the Centre, the PPP, mainly over the recent elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK). On Monday, PPP’s Sharmila Farooqui summed her party’s position in a post on X, saying: “No PPP, no quorum, simple.” She later told Dawn that PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had already made it clear that the party would “no more cooperate with PML-N on quorum and legislation” until its concerns over the AJK polls were addressed. When the matter was raised during Sadiq’s interaction with the media in Islamabad on Tuesday, he said: “Some ministers told me that the matter was taken up with the prime minister sahib yesterday […] The prime minister has taken notice, and the ministers will also ensure quorum”. He expressed hope that more lawmakers would now attend the proceedings. “I believe it will get better; there was improvement today, and I hope it will [further] improve in the next session because I have received a message from the government that there is a realisation on the issue.” Sadiq also said it was the government and the opposition’s responsibility to maintain quorum. The speaker urged lawmakers from opposition and treasury benches to utilise the forum of Parliament to highlight the issues of their constituencies rather than “abandoning” it, as doing so would be a collective loss. When a reporter asked if he was “worried that a no-confidence motion may be moved against him given that a similar claim was being made in the media regarding PM Shehbaz,” Sadiq said: “It is their (opposition’s) constitutional right, and we will facilitate it should they want to move such a motion. We will see when the time comes”. Asked about his invitation to the opposition for talks, the speaker said PM Shehbaz had extended such invitations several times, and he, along with Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar and Adviser to PM on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, had also made efforts to engage with the opposition. “I am tired of saying this. If they want to come, they will come. We can request the government as well, but how many times can we say the same thing?” he remarked.

Body of missing five-year-old girl recovered in KP’s Haripur: police. PESHAWAR: Police and rescue officials on Monday night recovered the body of a girl who had gone missing from outside her home in a semi-urban area of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Haripur district two weeks ago. According to rescue and medical sources, the body was buried after an autopsy. The detailed post-mortem report was awaited. District Headquarters Hospital Medical Superintendent Dr Munawar Afridi said the board of female doctors that conducted the autopsy was still compiling the post-mortem report. “It would therefore be premature to determine the nature of injuries sustained by the victim or the exact cause of her death,” he told Dawn . Speaking to the media at a press conference in Haripur on Tuesday, District Police Officer (DPO) Shafiullah Gandapur said the five-year-old went missing from outside her home at around 6pm on Aug 10. Police initially began an inquiry under Section 156(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code ( CrPC ), which deals with investigations into cognisable cases, and formally registered a first information report (FIR) under Section 364-A of the Pakistan Penal Code ( PPC ), relating to kidnapping or abduction with intent to murder, on Aug 12. The move followed the collection of CCTV footage and geofencing of the area, according to police. The DPO said police had initially arrested three suspects, one of whom recorded a confessional statement before a duty magistrate on Saturday. According to the statement, four suspects were involved in abducting the girl and taking her to an area near Model Town, where the suspect and another accused allegedly sexually assaulted her. According to Gandapur, none of the three suspects initially arrested by police disclosed where they had left the victim after the assault. However, during a search of the area, police obtained CCTV footage from another house, which helped them trace a fourth suspect. Acting on information provided by the fourth suspect, police recovered the five-year-old’s body from an unused well at a warehouse near one of the link roads leading to Haripur University, the DPO said. He said the suspect had thrown the victim into the well after allegedly raping her and had attempted to conceal the body with foliage. The DPO added doctors had collected body samples for DNA and forensic analysis. Responding to a question, he described the case as “sensitive and complex” and said a local team of investigators, including Superintendent of Police (SP) Security Samina Zafar and women officers from the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and IT wings, had diligently traced the suspects and recovered the body. Three of the suspects had been sent to prison on judicial remand, while the fourth was being interrogated to gather further evidence and bring all those involved to justice, he said. “We have not closed the investigation as we expect some more details,” he added. KP Chief Minister Muhammad Sohail Afridi also took notice of the incident and expressed deep sorrow and strong condemnation in a statement on Tuesday. He directed that a special investigation team be formed to probe the matter. He termed the incident “sad and heartbreaking”, adding that those responsible would be given “the strictest punishment according to the law”. Afridi expressed his sympathies and condolences to the girl’s family, saying, “Such heinous crimes against children will not be tolerated under any circumstances.” Workers of different political parties and civil society organisations had blocked Haripur’s GT Road on Sunday to protest the delay in the recovery of the girl, expressing a lack of confidence in the investigation.

Opposition, govt spar in Senate over Imran Khan’s medical treatment. ISLAMABAD: The opposition and the government on Tuesday sparred in the Senate over the treatment of PTI founder and former premier Imran Khan in hospital, with both sides accusing each other of contempt of a Supreme Court (SC) order . On August 18, the apex court ordered the government to shift the PTI founder to the Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad and to constitute a medical board, including his sister and personal physician. However, instead of shifting Imran to the Shifa Hospital, the government took him to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), citing security concerns and shifted him back to the Adiala jail after the medical board declared him medically fit. The PTI and Imran’s family have been accusing the government of not implementing the SC’s order of shifting him to Shifa Hospital. The heated argument broke out on Tuesday after presiding officer Shahadat Awan disallowed the opposition from moving a resolution concerning the implementation of the SC’s order regarding Imran’s medical treatment at Shifa International Hospital, but allowed discussion on points of order. The opposition slammed the government for what it called “throwing the binding orders of the SC in the dustbin”, while the government insisted that it was for the court to determine whether the verdict had been implemented. The session, chaired by PPP Senator Shahadat Awan, ruled that the matter was sub judice and could only be raised through a point of order, not a resolution. PTI parliamentary leader Barrister Ali Zafar, who sought to move a resolution, said the Senate must uphold the “supremacy of the Constitution” and reaffirm its commitment to implementing SC orders. Speaking on the floor of the house, Zafar cited the SC’s Aug 18 order directing the authorities to take Imran to Shifa International Hospital for treatment and constitute a medical board. “Neither was he taken to Shifa Hospital nor was a board constituted. Even a machine to check his heart was not available at Pims,” Zafar alleged. “Can any government refuse to implement a Supreme Court order? No, it cannot,” he said, referring to Articles 190 and 204 of the Constitution, which make compliance with court orders binding and non-compliance contempt of court. “You may oppose Imran Khan’s politics. Do that. But do not play politics with his health,” he added. “Governments come and go, but the Constitution remains.” PTI Senator Azam Swati accused the government of double standards. “When someone has to be given a benefit, relief is provided in judicial matters. Institutions were sent to Islamabad airport to give relief to Nawaz Sharif,” he said. Responding on behalf of the government, Adviser to the Prime Minister Rana Sanaullah said the state was “subject to the Constitution” and had complied with the SC order. “The court also said security arrangements would be assessed by the administration. Given the law and order situation, he was taken to a government hospital where qualified doctors were available,” he said. Sanaullah said a doctors’ panel had examined the PTI founder and declared his health “satisfactory”, after which he was sent back to jail. “The matter is before the court. The report will be submitted on Sept 16. Let the court examine it and decide whether the order was implemented.” He questioned why the opposition was “determined to prove him ill” when his own doctors and family had said he was in good health. “Do not do politics on health. If you are telling us not to, then you should also refrain,” he said. Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas called on the government to show “magnanimity” and implement the court order “in letter and spirit”. He proposed that a Senate committee be formed to visit the jail. “Politics and politicians are being crushed. Who will run the country then? It is not too late. There is no benefit in contempt of court,” he said.

Petroleum division kicks off feasibility study on strategic reserves. ISLAMABAD: The government on Tuesday kicked off a feasibility study regarding strategic petroleum reserves (SPR) through international consultancy firm Wood McKenzie. Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervaiz Malik today chaired the kick-off meeting with Wood Mackenzie, which was selected to undertake the study following a competitive tender process that attracted four bids. Wood Mackenzie Vice President Christopher Darry, Director Chris Brown, Principal Consultant Jordan Macdonald and Senior Vice President Aamir Malik attended the meeting. Representatives of Attock Refinery Limited, the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics, Government Holdings (Private) Limited, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Pakistan LNG Limited were also present. “The minister was briefed on the scope and objectives of the study, following which the meeting discussed and agreed on the timelines and overall architecture for the assignment,” an official statement by the information ministry said. The minister highlighted that the government was pursuing reforms and initiatives to advance Pakistan’s energy security, recognising that energy security was intrinsically linked to national security. He termed ensuring the resilience of energy supplies and reducing vulnerabilities to external shocks a key priority of the government, according to the statement. He said the recent crisis in the Strait of Hormuz had further magnified the need to strengthen Pakistan’s buffers and build greater resilience against supply disruptions. “The SPR initiative is therefore an important step towards assessing how the country can strengthen its preparedness for potential supply shocks,” he said, noting that the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) had already approved a “world-class bonded scheme” for large international oil players. The government on Monday formally approved allowing foreign fuel suppliers to set up bonded storage facilities in Pakistan at their own expense for multiple purposes, including re-export and supplies to the local market. Malik said the purpose of commissioning the study was to enable the government to make an informed decision based on evidence before embarking on such a major strategic initiative. The minister also emphasised that the study should provide a “pragmatic and implementable” solution suited to the country’s requirements and help to determine the most appropriate way forward, the statement said. This would include the possibility of pursuing SPR development in a phased manner. According to the statement, the Wood Mackenzie team termed it the “right time” for Pakistan to work on energy security, particularly in view of the evolving global energy landscape and recent supply disruptions. The team said the study would focus on developing a pragmatic solution based on Pakistan’s specific requirements and circumstances. “The study will cover technical feasibility, integrity, safety and operational assessment of proposed strategic storage facilities; international and regional benchmarks; policy and regulatory requirements; and short-, medium- and long-term implementation options,” the statement said. “It will also examine legal, regulatory, financial, commercial and institutional arrangements, including possible public-private partnership models.” The study will assess existing infrastructure that could potentially be utilised for strategic storage, taking into account connectivity and logistics requirements, the statement noted. It will also provide “estimates of capital expenditure, financing options, implementation timelines and institutional responsibilities for phased development of SPR capacity” in Pakistan. The minister directed all relevant stakeholders to extend full cooperation to Wood Mackenzie, ensuring the timely provision of required data and input to allow the completion of the study within agreed timelines and “provide a sound basis for future policy decisions”. He added that a steering committee will be formed to periodically review progress on this matter. Pakistan has been planning to boost domestic storage for crude oil and refined products to increase its energy security, it emerged in May. With no strategic petroleum reserves, the country has been left exposed to oil supply shocks resulting from the US-Iran war that has choked supplies through the Strait of Hormuz . In July, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif directed authorities to increase the country’s strategic petroleum reserves as a cabinet committee approved amendments to the oil refining policy.

‘Patience has run out’: JI warns of shutdown, Islamabad march if petroleum levy not abolished. LAHORE: Jamaat-i-Islami Pakistan Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Tuesday once again warned of a nationwide shutdown, road blockades and a march on Islamabad if the government failed to withdraw the petroleum levy. Addressing a press conference at the JI sit-in outside the Punjab chief minister’s House in Lahore, Rehman said the protests had entered their 10th day and were gaining momentum across the country. “The people’s patience has run out,” he said, demanding the immediate withdrawal of the petroleum levy and what he described as unjustified taxes. He said the ongoing sit-ins would continue until the government provided meaningful relief to the public. Rehman said the JI would announce the date for a nationwide strike on 13th Rabi-ul-Awwal, while protests would continue during Eid Miladun Nabi celebrations. He said the party had mobilised people across all four provinces and would expand the campaign if its demands were ignored. The JI chief said the government and those running the system had failed to address the country’s economic problems, adding that successive decisions had shifted the burden of the state’s failures onto ordinary citizens. “Governments in other countries have increased fuel prices only marginally even amid war conditions, but our rulers have turned the war into an opportunity to make money,” he said. The JI chief demanded the immediate abolition of the petroleum levy and other taxes on fuel, saying commuters, students, labourers and motorcyclists were struggling to cope with rising costs. He also called for the price of roti to be reduced to Rs10. Rehman also raised questions over alleged irregularities in coal imported for independent power producers (IPPs), calling for a forensic audit of the entire process. He said the Power Division had itself acknowledged irregularities in coal-related transactions and demanded an independent investigation to determine who had benefited from the alleged malpractice. The JI leader said consumers were being forced to pay for expensive fuel, electricity that was not generated and questionable IPP arrangements. He added that the public was ultimately bearing the cost of government and elite extravagance. Referring to the JI’s previous campaign against IPPs, Rehman said public pressure had contributed to a reduction of around Rs10 per unit in electricity prices. He warned that the JI would intensify its protests if the government failed to respond to its demands. “Shutdowns, road blockades and a march on Islamabad are among our options,” he said, adding that the government should not test the party’s resolve. Rehman also criticised the political system, saying governments lacking genuine public support remained weak. Referring to the ruling coalition as a “Form-47 product”, he said it had failed to resolve the problems confronting ordinary Pakistanis. He added that the PPP had damaged Sindh and criticised what he described as a family monopoly in Punjab. He also questioned the failure to hold local government elections for years. Criticising the Punjab government, Rehman said its much-publicised initiatives could not conceal its failure to address fundamental issues. Rehman stressed that the JI was protesting not for personal or political interests but for the rights of the people. He invited the government’s negotiating committee to visit the protest camp and explain when the petroleum levy would be withdrawn and how relief would be provided to the public. “We will not go to Islamabad merely to receive a briefing from any committee,” he said. Speaking about a recent incident involving a security official at Islamabad’s Sarhad University of Science and Information Technology (SUSIT), the JI emir said the matter should be dealt with strictly according to law. He called for a merit-based investigation and action against anyone found responsible, regardless of their position or influence. JI Acting Secretary General Nazir Ahmed Janjua, Deputy Secretary Russel Khan Babar, JI Lahore Emir Ziauddin Ansari, JI Central Punjab Emir Javed Qasoori and Information Secretary Shakil Ahmed Tarabi were also present at the press conference.

Apple launches faster Mac mini, Mac Studio to tap AI boom. Apple on Tuesday unveiled a more powerful Mac mini aimed at consumers looking to host AI agents remotely, marking what is likely the final product launch of Tim Cook’s tenure as CEO. The new mini, unveiled alongside a beefed-up Mac Studio, starts at $899 and comes with either Apple’s new M6 chip or the M5 Pro. It is $100 more expensive than its predecessor. Both devices have become popular with consumers looking to run autonomous AI agents such as OpenClaw locally, with high demand depleting inventories at several Apple stores. “Whether it’s being used as a home computer, powering a professional studio, or as an always-on agentic device, it’s the little Mac that can do it all,” the company’s hardware boss Johny Srouji said. The unveiling is likely Apple’s last major launch before Tim Cook hands over the reins to hardware veteran John Ternus in one of its most closely watched leadership transitions. It also highlights mounting cost pressures as memory chip prices climb on strong demand from AI data centres, which prompted Apple to raise prices on some Mac and iPad models in June . One variant of the new mini is powered by Apple’s 2-nanometer M6 chip, which the company said delivers up to four times faster AI performance and double the graphics and storage speeds compared with the previous M4-powered model. The higher-end variant, powered by its M5 Pro chip, offers up to an 18-core central processor and 20-core graphics processor, targeting professional users working on tasks such as visual effects. Apple also refreshed its Mac Studio desktop lineup, introducing versions powered by its M5 Max and new M5 Ultra chips. Aimed at developers and other professional users, the machines can run large models on-device and combine the computing power of multiple systems for more intensive AI tasks. Pricing starts at $2,499 for the M5 Max version and $5,499 for the M5 Ultra model, up from $1,999 for the previous generation.

Speaker, deputy speaker take oath after election to AJK Assembly. MUZAFFARABAD: Chaudhary Tariq Farooq of the PML-N was elected the 16th speaker of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Legislative Assembly, while party colleague Muhammad Ahmed Raza Qadri was elected deputy speaker, in elections to both offices held on Tuesday. The session started at 2:30pm, with outgoing Speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar of the PPP in the chair. Akbar could not retain his seat in the recent general elections. The PPP had fielded Chaudhry Qasim Majeed and Aamir Abdul Ghaffar Lone for the two offices. All 46 legislators — 32 from the PML-N and its ally and 14 from the PPP — who had taken oath on Monday participated in the polling. Farooq, elected from LA-7 (Bhimber City), secured 32 votes, while Majeed, elected from LA-2 (Chakswari), received 13 votes, with one PPP vote being rejected. The rejected vote was reportedly cast by PPP lawmaker Zobia Khurshid Raja, who was elected to a women’s reserved seat through a draw of lots after her votes had equalled those of PML-N candidate Riffat Abid. After Majeed and some other PPP lawmakers pointed out that Raja’s vote had been rejected, she reportedly told a colleague that she had marked a tick rather than a cross on the ballot paper. Farooq was then administered the oath by his predecessor. PML-N leader Raja Farooq Haider, whose camaraderie with Akbar is well known, paid rich tribute to him for running the House smoothly. He highlighted that he and Akbar were the last members of the outgoing Assembly who had also been elected in 1985, following the restoration of democracy in AJK and Pakistan. PPP regional president Chaudhry Muhammad Yasin also paid what he described as a “big tribute” to Akbar, praising his unflinching commitment to the PPP and democracy. Farooq later conducted the election for deputy speaker, which was won by Qadri with 32 votes. Interestingly, Lone also secured 13 votes, with one PPP vote being rejected again, prompting speculation within the party about whether the rejection was deliberate rather than accidental. Farooq then administered the oath to Qadri as deputy speaker. Both Qadri and Lone belong to Kashmiri refugee constituencies — the former from Rawalpindi and the latter from Karachi. The PML-N had reportedly earlier decided to field Raja Asif of LA-11 (Sehnsa) for the slot, but he declined the offer. The PPP had initially nominated Zaffar Iqbal Malik of LA-8 (Raj Mahal) before changing its decision and fielding Lone. Members from both sides made brief speeches congratulating Farooq on his election and expressing good wishes. Alongside Haider, among those who spoke were PML-N president Shah Ghulam Qadir, Syed Shoukat Shah, Sehrish Qamar, Pir Mazhar Saeed and Qadri. PPP members also spoke, including Yasin, Majeed, outgoing prime minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore, Abdul Majid Khan, Mian Abdul Waheed and Deevan Ali Chughtai. They expressed the hope that the new speaker would ensure impartiality in conducting the proceedings and provide adequate space to both the treasury and opposition benches to voice their concerns. Former law minister Mian Abdul Waheed said Farooq had earned the office through his political struggle, hard work and contribution to the parliamentary system. “You got this office on merit, owing to your political struggle, hard work and valuable contribution to the system. I congratulate your party for elevating you to this office,” he said. Farooq, a Bhimber resident who defeated former prime minister Chaudhry Anwarul Haq by a margin of more than 12,000 votes, is the PML-N’s regional secretary general. He is regarded as a well-versed and articulate politician who regularly engages with party workers and the wider public through social media platforms. He also has close connections with the Kashmiri diaspora in the UK and Europe. Several prominent members of the diaspora, including Ateeque-ur-Rehman, a former mayor of Oldham, travelled to AJK to attend his swearing-in ceremony. His election and oath-taking were witnessed from the visitors’ gallery by all three of his wives and his children. Speaking at the conclusion of the session, Farooq thanked members from both sides and said the office demanded impartiality. “In a democratic society, the role of the opposition is very important. To me, all members carry equal importance regardless of their affiliations, and I will ensure they get maximum possible opportunity to voice the sentiments of their electorate and problems of their constituencies concerned,” he said. “I will leave no stone unturned to maintain the dignity, honour and sanctity of this House,” he vowed. Since the office of the AJK president has remained vacant since January, Farooq will also serve as acting president, as did his predecessor, until the election of a new president. Meanwhile, the schedule for the election of the leader of the House was also issued on Tuesday. According to the schedule, nomination papers will be submitted and scrutinised on Thursday, followed by polling the same day. The newly elected leader of the House will take oath before the acting president at the High Court ground on Thursday afternoon.

Imran's hospital transfer: SC to take up Dr Uzma's contempt plea on Sept 16. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court will take up on Sept 16 a contempt of court petition filed by Dr Uzma Khan against the government for allegedly violating its Aug 18 directions to transfer incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad. The same three-member bench, comprising Justice Shahid Waheed, Justice Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim, which issued the Aug 18 order, will hear the contempt plea filed by Imran’s sister. On Sept 16, the bench was also scheduled to resume hearing the pending cases concerning the former premier’s health and issues related to family meetings. However, it is not clear whether the same bench will also take up the review petition filed by the Islamabad chief commissioner, challenging the court’s directions to shift PTI founder Imran Khan to a private hospital. An informed source told Dawn that early fixation of the case was not possible because 94 criminal original petitions of the same category were pending before different SC benches. Under the fixation policy, cases are required to be fixed for hearing in their turn within the relevant category. It is therefore unlikely that the contempt case will come up before Sept 16, the source said. However, since the main case concerning Imran’s health is pending for hearing on Sept 16, the contempt petition is also expected to be taken up on the same date, the source added. Earlier in the day, the PTI resubmitted the contempt of court petition by PTI founder sister to the SC’s registrar against the alleged violation of its Aug 18 order. Later, Imran’s sister Uzma Khan also filed an application for the early hearing of the contempt petition. The contempt plea was re-submitted shortly after the SC returned it after raising certain objections. PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan said that the SC registrar had informed him that the petition was being returned, with one of the objections being that the list of charges levelled against the respondents had not been dispatched. He had also said that the PTI was going to resubmit the petition after removing the objections raised. Last week, Imran’s sister Uzma Khan had filed a petition before the SC against the authorities for violating the court’s Aug 18 order. In its order, the court had ordered the government to shift Imran to Shifa International Hospital, a private facility, within two days for examination and treatment by a multidisciplinary medical board. However, the government instead took the PTI founder to Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), a government hospital, for a check-up and then subsequently transported back to prison. At the time, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar had blamed “the security situation created by PTI workers on the way to and outside” the hospital for the diversion. In her petition, Uzma — who was present for the check-up — had named Islamabad Chief Commissioner (retired) Lieutenant Sohail Ashraf, Interior Secretary Ahmed Raza Sarwar, Punjab Inspector General Prisons Mian Salik Jalal, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar as respondents. She had alleged that the respondents had committed wilful, deliberate and contumacious disobedience and violation of the order. She had also requested the apex court to depute an officer or appoint a local commission to ensure that Imran was immediately shifted to the private hospital in accordance with its earlier directions. At the same time, the Islamabad chief commissioner had also approached the SC, seeking an early hearing of his review petition, in which the legality of the Aug 18 order was questioned. On Monday, Gohar had met the SC registrar and was assured that a bench would be constituted soon to proceed with the contempt of court petition. Responding to a question, he had also brushed aside the impression of any deal with the government, saying that the PTI founder did not make deals, otherwise he would not have spent three years in prison. Early hearing plea In her plea for an early hearing, Uzma highlighted that the matter at hand concerned the life, health, dignity and physical well-being of Imran, whose health was “deteriorating and whose life is stated to be in jeopardy”. “Every further delay may cause serious and irreparable harm,” the application said. The application stated that the Aug 18 court order was required to be obeyed forthwith and in letter and spirit. “The filing or pendency of any review petition on part of the chief commissioner does not, by itself, suspend or dilute the binding force of the order unless its operation is expressly stayed by the Supreme Court,” the petition said. It added that respondents named in the contempt plea were legally required to act strictly in accordance with the directions of the Supreme Court. “If any genuine clarification or modification was considered necessary, the proper course was to approach the Supreme Court, rather than to depart from or substitute its express directions,” it argued. The applicant also expressed regret that “disobedience” by the respondents was “continuing in nature” and emphasised that this required “immediate judicial consideration so that the authority of the Supreme Court was upheld and its directions concerning the life and health of the prisoner were implemented without further loss of time”. “The applicant has a strong prima facie case and the balance of convenience lies entirely in favour of early fixation,” the application said, arguing that no prejudice would be caused to the respondents if the matter was heard at the earliest. However, it added, a delay may cause “irreparable loss and injury”. The application also cited media reports and recalled that the chief commissioner, in his review petition, had also prayed for an early hearing of his plea.

Imran Khan’s sister Noreen Niazi meets him in Adiala jail for second consecutive week. ISLAMABAD: Former prime minister Imran Khan’s sister, Noreen Niazi, met him at Adiala jail on Tuesday for the second consecutive week, in line with the Supreme Court’s (SC) directions. In response to Imran’s petition filed in May , the SC on August 18 ruled that meetings should be facilitated between the prisoner and his family members once a week. The court had also directed that the government would facilitate the prisoner in speaking to his sons by telephone twice a week. Following the SC’s directions, Imran’s family reassured the court that they would not speak to the media. According to PTI lawyer Awais Younas Chaudhry, Noreen’s meeting with Imran today lasted around 45 minutes. “Earlier, Bushra Bibi’s family was allowed to meet her, and then it was conveyed that Noreen Niazi could meet Imran Khan,” Chaudhry told Dawn . “The other two sisters were waiting in the vehicle. When Noreen Niazi came out of the jail, all the sisters left without speaking to the media,” he said. Chaudhry said that PTI was following the guidelines and orders of the apex court. Noreen had also met Imran last Tuesday, on August 18. “We really appreciate the role of the Supreme Court as the meetings with PTI’s founding chairman have become possible only because of the court,” Chaudhry said. He said he hoped the government would implement the court orders in full and shift Imran to Shifa International Hospital for medical treatment, where his personal physicians would be allowed to examine him. However, the government instead took the PTI founder to Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), a government hospital, for a check-up and then subsequently transported back to prison. At the time, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar had blamed “the security situation created by PTI workers on the way to and outside” the hospital for the diversion. In October 2025, the Islamabad High Court directed the Adiala jail superintendent to implement a March 24 order that reinstated the twice-a-week meeting schedule for the PTI founder. The ex-premier’s family and party had repeatedly accused prison authorities of “ sabotaging ” meetings with him.

Govt forms high-powered body to break deadlock over Iran-Pakistan gas pipeline amid penalty threats. ISLAMABAD: With millions of dollars in potential penalties looming, the government has constituted a high-powered committee to find a “mutually acceptable” way out of the decades-old impasse over the Pakistan-Iran gas pipeline, as it weighs the cost of penalties against the country’s growing energy needs. Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik told the Senate on Tuesday that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had set up the committee to examine the project’s legal, financial and energy dimensions and recommend a way forward “in Pakistan’s national interest”. Raising an attention notice, Senator Talha Mahmood noted that the project had been delayed for two decades and that Iran had already laid the pipeline up to the Pakistani border. He asked whether Pakistan was ready to receive Iranian gas once sanctions were lifted and how much work had been completed on its side of the pipeline. “Can Pakistan immediately integrate Iranian gas into its system? How long will it take to make the pipeline operational after sanctions are lifted? What preparations has Pakistan made to receive the gas?” he asked. The senator further asked whether the infrastructure for transporting Iranian gas had been completed and what practical progress had been made on the project. Malik said the matter had gone into arbitration in Paris under the Gas Sales Purchase Agreement signed between the two countries in 2009. Under the agreement, Pakistan was to complete its 781km pipeline by December 2014. The deadline was later extended, but Islamabad could not begin construction on its territory due to US sanctions and a lack of financing. Iran completed its section years ago. In 2023, Tehran served a formal notice seeking damages for the delay , with reports suggesting the claim could run into billions of dollars. The dispute is now being heard by an international arbitration tribunal in Paris. “The committee is looking at the potential liability facing Pakistan, the implications of litigation and the country’s future energy requirements,” the petroleum minister told the house. “These factors will help determine the way forward on the project.” He added that the government wanted to avoid further complications from litigation and was therefore pursuing a negotiated settlement with Tehran. “Iran is a brotherly country and the leadership of the two countries remains engaged in efforts to reach an amicable settlement acceptable to both sides,” the minister said. Malik noted that Iran had already made “substantial physical progress” on its side of the pipeline, having brought gas from the South Pars field to a major city near the Pakistani border. The petroleum minister also addressed concerns over gas supply problems in Balochistan. He said the prime minister had directed him to engage with provincial stakeholders. He informed the house that another high-level committee, headed by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, was examining Balochistan’s gas-related problems, including technical faults and payment issues. In May 2009, Pakistan and Iran signed an agreement for the supply of 750 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) of gas for 25 years from Iran’s South Pars gas field. Both countries were required to implement the project in their respective territories. According to the agreement, the project was to start supply by January 2015.

Indepe­ndent power producers found overcharging users through costly coal procurement. ISLAMABAD: Indepe­ndent power producers (IPPs) operating on impor­ted coal have been found imposing an additional burden on electricity consumers through opaque and inefficient coal procurement practices, with the cost ultimately passed on through monthly fuel price adjustments (FPAs). While consumer groups have been raising concerns over such practices at various forums, including public hearings, the power division and the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) have now also pointed to inefficiencies in coal procurement and their financial impact on consumers. The issue gained prominence after recent competitive bidding for coal supply to the 660MW state-owned Jamshoro Power Plant attracted a discount of $7.12 per tonne from a Karachi-based supplier compared to discounts of only 20 to 50 cents per tonne in some contracts involving IPPs. “The power division has identified significant inefficiencies in the procurement of imported coal by power plants,” an official statement said on Tuesday, adding that fresh policy guidelines had been iss­ued “for corrective action that could save the natio­nal exchequer up to Rs380 million annually”. In a recent order, Nepra had already pointed out concerns over coal procurement by Port Qasim Electric Power Company (PQEPC) under a six-year contract involving discounts of $0.20 to $0.50 per tonne based on estimated coal prices. “This type of evaluation has never been observed in any bidding by any other power plant, including PQEPC, and does not seem justified, as it is based on estimated coal prices, which may change in future,” Nepra said in its judgement. The regulator also noted that the Port Qasim plant had published its tender notice only in China instead of reaching out to a broader pool of potential bidders. “Had discounts been incorporated into the bid evaluation as a major criterion, it may have yielded more competitive and higher discounts from prospective bidders,” Nepra said. The regulator also observed that the plant had not disclosed that it had already executed a long-term coal supply agreement when the matter was discussed with the regulator on two occasions, prompting “proceedings regarding misstatement and/or non-disclosure of information”. Nepra subsequently directed the Port Qasim plant to conduct fresh bidding for a long-term coal supply agreement within three months of its March 2026 FPA decision. However, officials said that after the March 25 order, the company procured about 1.2 million tonnes of coal, enough for almost an entire year, just before a new tender. They said the contract again involved a discount of around $0.50 per tonne against the $7.12 discount secured by the public-sector Jamshoro plant. The difference alone works out to around $8 million, officials said. If similar procurement practices were followed by other IPPs, the impact could rise substantially. The power division said the procurement inefficiencies were identified during a series of meetings presided over by the power minister, where officials reviewed actual data, contractual arrangements and market practices. “Pakistan has a significant fleet of coal-fired power plants with a combined capacity of approximately 5,280 megawatts that rely wholly or partly on imported coal. These include three major 1,320MW plants at Port Qasim, Hub Power and Sahiwal, as well as the Lucky and Jamshoro plants which also have the capability to use imported coal,” it said. The division said coal import prices for IPPs were linked to internationally recognised benchmarks such as the API-4 index, but the final price paid by a plant also depended on the discount negotiated with the supplier. PQEPC Chief Financial Officer Adil Ashraf and Procurement Chief Liang Ding Ping did not respond to Dawn’s written queries. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

France permanently closes consulate in Karachi. KARACHI: The Consulate General of France in Karachi is closing its doors permanently after 50 years of service. This was announced by the outgoing French Ambassador to Pakistan Nicolas Galey at a farewell organised by the Board of Management of the Quaid-i-Azam House Museum in collaboration with the Karachi Council of Foreign Relations on Tuesday. The event was aimed at saying goodbye to two great friends of Pakistan: Ambassador Galey and the Consul General of France in Karachi Alexis Chahtahtinsky. The ambassador said that he was also feeling a bit sad after spending almost five years in Pakistan. Farewell held for French Ambassador Nicolas Galey and Consul General Alexis Chahtahtinsky “And my leaving is also coinciding with the departure of our Consul General in Karachi Alexis Chahtahtinsky. Someone will replace me in Islamabad but here in Karachi, the French Consulate, which opened in 1976, is closing down after 50 years of service,” he said. “I have visited Karachi many times and have seen the vitality of this city. I have seen it changing and improving,” he said, while appreciating Consul General Alexis for his good work in Karachi. “Even though the consulate is closing, there is still the Alliance Francaise, which will now serve as our flagship. There will also be the Pakistan France Business Alliance here doing its work,” the Ambassador reminded. He also said that he really appreciates Pakistan’s efforts in at least getting “a kind of ceasefire in the Gulf. Pakistan has emerged as a very influential country in difficult circumstances.” Consul General Chahtahtinsky said that he was leaving Karachi and Pakistan on September 1. “I am going back to France but I am taking great memories of Karachi with me,” he said, adding that he is not just a great friend but also an old friend of Pakistan. “I first visited Pakistan as a student in 1983, which was a great thing, because as a diplomat you don’t get so much freedom to go where you want. I was lucky enough to visit and fall in love with the Northern Areas of Pakistan at the time,” he said. “As the Consul General, I spent another four memorable years in Karachi, which was the first capital of Pakistan and still its economic hub. Indeed, Karachi, as the biggest port in the country, is the gateway to Pakistan,” he said. “It is a great place for doing business and has a great social life. I will always have a special place in my heart for Karachi,” he added. “Earlier Pakistan had a reputation of crime and terrorism and embassy people used to be afraid to come here. But since February 28, when the major conflict erupted in the Gulf, Pakistan has also emerged on the world map due to its mediation efforts. The entire world is grateful to Pakistan for its role. It is a very different Pakistan that we are leaving. Instead of being a problem, Pakistan has repositioned itself to become part of the solution,” the consul general said. During his vote of thanks, Vice Chairman of the Board of Management of the Karachi Council of Foreign Relations Ikram Sehgal recounted that France was the first non-Muslim nation to recognise Pakistan though diplomatic relations between both countries were established in 1951. “France has lent Pakistan support whenever we needed it. We got Daphne-class submarines followed by the Agosta-class submarines at a time when no one was giving us weapons. “Before that we had the Mirage III and Mirage 5 fighter jets. Through Project Retrofit of Strike Element [ROSE], a modernisation programme for ageing Mirage jets carried out at the Pakistan Aeronautical Complex in Kamra, we are still flying their upgraded versions. In between, we also captured some French army tanks used by India to put into use ourselves,” he said, adding that France is wrong in closing its consulate in Karachi at this time when Pakistan’s waters are turning into a major power. “This is a time when France could have taken advantage of the opportunities coming up here in the name of trade and new alliances are coming up geopolitically as Pakistan gets ready to play a big role,” he concluded. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs343.10 per litre while HSD will cost Rs371.80 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to a Petroleum Division notification, the new prices will be applicable on Aug 26 (Wednesday) and 27 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Dual approach. WITH regard to resolving the US-Iran stand-off, two distinct approaches are being pursued simultaneously. The more mature track involves Pakistan and other regional countries that are trying to revive the Islamabad MoU and ensure a peaceful denouement to this crisis. In this regard, Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir was in Tehran on Monday for talks with the Iranian leadership . The other — more combative — approach involves the US ramping up financial pressure on Iran through sanctions and what it calls an “economic onslaught”. The US on Monday announced a fresh set of sanctions targeting Iran under the imaginatively titled ‘Operation Economic Outcast’. Field Marshal Munir met the Iranian president, as well as other top leaders, in Tehran. One of the positive outcomes of this interaction was Iran’s affirmation that it remains committed to the Islamabad MoU. However, as the Iranian national security chief said, “we distrust America”. This mutual distrust remains the biggest obstacle in operationalising the MoU. The reality is that America’s ramping up sanctions on Iran will do little to build bridges with Tehran. If anything, it will harden attitudes there. It should be remembered that Iran has survived punishing US sanctions for nearly half a century, and while the new curbs may increase the pain, they are unlikely to make Tehran yield. Moreover, there is little appetite amongst Iran’s major trading partners, particularly China, to toe Washington’s line. The announcement of new economic curbs is also an admission from the US that its strategy of defeating Iran on the battlefield has failed. The fact that the Iranians are willing to engage with mediators, and are still interested in reviving the Islamabad MoU, means that a peaceful way out of this crisis can be found. After the CDF’s visit, the Omani foreign minister was in Tehran yesterday to discuss the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. If the Trump administration goes ahead with its ill-advised plan to further isolate Iran economically, or if it considers restarting military action, it will undoubtedly attract a matching response from Iran. Very few states in the region want a return to hostilities. Therefore, both sides, particularly the US, need to take advantage of the renewed diplomatic push, and attempt to implement the salient features of the MoU. The US should drop its hostile rhetoric and attempt to reach a genuine understanding with Iran. Washington’s aggression against the Islamic Republic has proved a disaster, and it would be best for the US to quickly exit the quagmire with whatever remains of its tattered honour. The Iranians, meanwhile, should restore the free flow of marine traffic through Hormuz, and rebuild damaged ties with their Arab Gulf neighbours. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

Fresh efforts at mediation revive hopes for US-Iran climbdown. COMMERCIAL vessels are seen in the Strait of Hormuz, near the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas, as Tehran and Muscat agreed on a phased arrangement for the troubled waterway. According to the two sides, the agreement covers the formation of a temporary joint navigation corridor, mine clearance, information exchange and traffic management.—Reuters • Back-to-back Tehran trips by CDF Munir, Omani FM yield progress on key issues • Despite public brinkmanship, Washington ‘ready to show flexibility’ on economic sanctions if Iran meets ‘certain conditions’, US media reports • Diplomatic sources point to ‘softer than expected’ sanctions, say Islamabad taking the lead in conveying messages from Tehran to Washington, and vice versa • Iran seeks return to terms agreed in Islamabad MoU; eyes Hormuz agreement with Oman ISLAMABAD / WASHINGTON: Progress made during two key visits to Tehran — by Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir and Omani Foreign Minister Badr Al-Busaidi — may have opened the first potentially workable pathway towards de-escalation in the Gulf, since the breakdown of the armistice secured through the Islamabad Memor­andum of Understanding (MoU). Although there has been no clear breakthrough yet, and fundamental differences persist between Iran and the United States, the latest diplomatic activity has brought the political and technical dimensions of the dispute back into focus. In Washington too, there seems to be a willingness to consider sanctions relief as part of a broa­der understanding with Tehran, provided Iran meets certain conditions. According to some US media reports, Washington has offered an end to economic sanctions and the naval blockade against Iran in exchange for Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping and halting attacks by Iran-aligned regional groups. However, the specific terms have not been publicly confirmed by Washington or Tehran. Importantly, unlike the period following the collapse of the June understanding, when the two sides were largely talking past each other and the crisis was bec­o­ming increasingly militarised, there is a renewed push towards establishing a new mechanism for maintaining the ceasefire. Observers believe Field Mars­hal Munir’s visit served to reopen channels bet­w­­een Tehran and Washington, through Islamabad. It is also noteworthy that the Iranian reaction to the visit was unusually positive, with Seyed Mehdi Tabatabaei, deputy for communications and information at the Iranian president’s office, describing it as “highly fruitful” and saying it had produced “highly valuable diplomatic achievements”. The CDF’s meeting with Gen Mohsen Rezaei — the Supreme Leader’s representative on the Supreme National Security Council – was particularly significant in testing whether the security side in Tehran was also prepared to join the renewed process. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), too, said the Iranian leadership appreciated Pakistan’s “constructive role and sincere efforts” for dialogue and de-escalation. But Tehran has so far not publicly indicated any readiness to make unilateral concessions to US, rather, the message emerging from the meetings was that Iran remains prepared to return to the understanding formalised under Islamabad MoU, provided Washington first addresses what Tehran considers its violations of the memorandum, and returns to implementing the understanding. ‘Softer than expected’ sanctions Diplomatic sources in Washington also confirmed that Pakistan’s mediation role is being supported from the top, with Field Marshal Munir remaining in touch with both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, complemented by working-level contacts between US and Pakistani officials. Asked whether Pakistan had conveyed any US proposals to Iran, sources confirmed that this was the case, adding that Tehran’s proposals have also been relayed to Washington, “along with their comments”. “So, they are not only facilitating but also [carrying out] mediation, which includes conveying their opinions as well,” sources said. The description is broadly consistent with reporting by CBS News and The Wall Street Journal , both of which have identified Pakistan as an important conduit between Washington and Tehran. As evidence of the impact this messaging is having on the Trump adm­in­­istration’s actions, diplomatic sources in Washin­gton pointed to the recent announcement of economic sanctions against Iran. Although the Trump administration had billed the sanctions as spelling an “ economic doomsday” for Tehran, diplomatic sources said: “The restrictions are softer than expected, and also, on the other side, there have been no recent attacks on Gulf states”. While the Treasury Department has announced new sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and vessels, but the list did not feature any of the Chinese financial institutions thought to be facilitating Iran’s oil trade. The Iranian position, nevertheless, remains conditional as it continues to regard the Islamabad MoU as the appropriate framework, but wants Washington to demonstrate through concrete action that it is prepared to honour its commitments. The dispute over Hormuz is, meanwhile, not being treated by Iran as a separate maritime issue rather it has been tied to the issues of sanctions, the US naval blockade and reciprocal implementation of the June understanding. Hormuz progress In this context, the progress made in Oman-Iran talks assumes greater significance. Al-Busaidi’s visit to Tehran produced some forward movement on navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, with the two sides agreeing on a phased arrangement. As per the joint statement, the understanding between Oman and Iran includes a temporary joint navigation corridor, mine clearance, information exchange and traffic management, while technical discussions would continue on a permanent navigation arrangement. Al-Busaidi said in a post on X after the meeting that he hoped the countries would “soon announce” the temporary corridor in the strait. “Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course,” he said. Technical negotiations will continue to determine a “permanent navigational corridor and future administration of the Strait, as well as a mechanism for information-sharing, traffic management, and the provision of relevant navigational and security services”, the earlier joint statement read. The announcement came as US President Donald Trump repeated claims on Truth Social that “all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz”, citing the US navy. “Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed… There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in full force and effect,” he added. Meanwhile, the Reuters news agency reported that Washington is beginning to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized amid tensions with Iran. The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially operate below full capacity. ‘Pakistan Idol’ in dark times. WATCHING the long-awaited finale of Pakistan Idol was a refreshing break from the country’s ongoing political turmoil and escalating regional tensions. It was a fascinating contest between half a dozen exceptionally talented young amateur artists from across Pakistan, selected from hundreds of contestants — many from the remotest corners — who had competed for nearly a year. I was completely hooked, and followed every episode on television. What struck me most was the raw talent of these young performers — especially the girls from small towns, fiercely determined to prove themselves on the national stage. Hira Qaisar took the title of Pakistan Idol. A mother of three from Faisalabad who has never had any formal music training, she held the judges and audience spellbound with her mastery of both classical and popular singing. Hira was certainly exceptional; stars like her are born every season. That brilliance is in stark contrast to the hopelessness and frustration that young people feel today. With few opportunities and rising unemployment, they are leaving the country — many by illegal means, risking their lives in the hope of a better future. Hundreds die on the way and still they keep trying. It is hard to imagine a worse outlook for a nation where roughly 64 per cent of the population is under 30. Around four million people are added to the population every year, while 25m children are out of school, one of the highest numbers globally. Even among those enrolled, many can hardly read or write. The country is producing an ever-larger pool of undereducated, unskilled citizens. Youth unemployment is far higher than the national average. Pakistan is facing a severe youth crisis, and events like Pakistan Idol offer only a fleeting moment of pride. A youth bulge is a huge source of talent, but only if provided with education, jobs and a functioning state. Right now, it doesn’t have these. The system has failed to address the critical issues driving this crisis, and inaction has eroded young people’s belief that state institutions can deliver for them. We face a youth crisis of such severity that events like ‘Pakistan Idol’ are just a fleeting spark. Most disturbing of all is the collapse of the rule of law and the denial of basic democratic rights. An elite-dominated, extractive political system remains unresponsive to ordinary people, and the result is growing cynicism and radicalisation across society. What is unfolding in Balochistan, KP and Azad Kashmir is nothing less than a revolt of the youth against a repressive order and denial of basic democratic rights. The response of the state, which has relied on coercive force, has only aggravated the situation. Public discontent is growing, and it is tangible across the rest of the country as authoritarianism tightens its grip. New laws recently passed by parliament have further concentrated power in the hands of a single individual — ostensibly boosting the hybrid system. Yet such actions only render the system more vulnerable to implosion rather than strengthen it. It is a lesson of history we refuse to learn. Last week, we witnessed the blatant defiance of Supreme Court instructions that the imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan be admitted to a private hospital for a full medical checkup. Khan was taken to a government hospital, not the one ordered by the court. While this defiance is read as a sign of hubris, it also exposes the fault lines within the hybrid system. A government of questionable legitimacy appears so afraid of popular backlash that it will not even allow the former prime minister to be admitted to a hospital for a medical checkup. There is also the question of whose decision it was to ignore the court order. The issue of Khan’s hospital transfer has now become a major flashpoint between the government and the opposition. In fact, it has divided the government itself. This is now a test for the Supreme Court, whose own independence has been drastically curtailed. In the past, prime ministers have been removed for defying the court’s orders. Can history be repeated? Many doubt it will be, given that the independence of the judiciary has already been compromised. But the incident has heightened political tensions in the country, and those who had bet on the fall of the government by the end of the year are now willing to raise the stakes. Given the historical unpredictability of Pakistani politics, one must not rule out any possibility, however far-fetched it may sound at the moment. Pakistan’s role in the emerging defence architecture of West Asia, defined by the newly signed trilateral Makkah Joint Defence Pact , has certainly raised the country’s regional profile. But Islamabad’s ambition to become a net security provider carries the risk of overstretching its military. It also risks being drawn into a wider conflict, given the escalating tensions driven by America’s unending war on Iran. Pakistan has managed its balancing act well so far, but it could flip as President Donald Trump declares an economic war on Iran. There is also the question of whether a fragile economy can bear the burden of overextended defence commitments. America’s latest economic war on Iran could draw China into the conflict too. Beijing has warned that it would safeguard its interests after Washington laid out plans for Iran’s “economic strangulation” . The statement came after the Trump administration threatened to impose penalties on countries, including China, if they breached the embargo. China is Iran’s biggest trading partner and has repeatedly stated that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions. “China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests,” the country’s foreign ministry asserted in a statement. Any confrontation between the two superpowers could endanger Pakistan’s delicate balancing act, given Islamabad’s close ties with both. Considering its political and economic instability, Pakistan can hardly afford to become part of a conflict that can damage its national security. It is high time the hybrid rulers defused political tensions, rather than fuelled them, by pursuing a policy of vengeance. There is also a need to focus on the real issues that confront the country. Authoritarian measures have only increased the vulnerability of the existing political order. Pakistan sits on $7tr mineral trove, claims planning minister. ISLAMABAD: Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has claimed that Pakistan estimates its mineral endowment at more than $7 trillion. Mr Iqbal made these remarks in a conversation with Farwa Amin, director for South Asian initiatives at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York, as per a statement issued by the planning ministry on Tuesday. The minister said large-scale mining operations required heavy up-front investments and extensive gestation periods, and the country’s volatile political climate was a primary deterrent to international resource developers. He said that with improved macroeconomic stability, the government was actively courting foreign partners, including US firms, through mechanisms such as the memorandum of understanding with US Strategic Metals, potential EXIM financing and participation in critical-minerals ministerial processes. Indus Water Treaty Mr Iqbal said India unilaterally held the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, describing it as the “first instance” in modern history of water being weaponised and creating a serious new security challenge for Pakistan. He said the 70-year-old treaty had remained “untouchable” even through multiple wars between the two countries. He warned that India could now deny Pakistan water when it was needed for crops and release it when it was not required, turning a shared resource into a potential instrument of pressure. He said Pakistan was accelerating construction of new reservoirs to create a strategic buffer, adding that the Diamer-Bhasha and Mohmand dams, once completed, would add roughly six million acre-feet of storage capacity. These projects are intended both to stabilise water supply against climate-driven variability and to reduce vulnerability to upstream manipulation, he said, adding that Islamabad was pursuing diplomatic channels to prevent the dispute from escalating into conflict. He also placed geoeconomics at the centre of Pakistan’s foreign policy under the “Uraan Pakistan” framework and the 5E strategy, arguing that the relationship with the United States in particular must move beyond the traditional security-geopolitics axis. Ties with US, China Mr Iqbal was equally clear that en­­gagement with the US would not come at the expense of China. He described China as a “trusted partner” that stepped in during Pakistan’s energy crisis with the first phase of the CPEC, delivering approximately $25 billion in investment that ended prolonged power shortages and upgraded highways, fibre-optic networks and Gwadar Port. Deputy Speaker Ghulam Shah showed great generosity by allowing more than three dozen members to speak on issues of their choice, after announcing that the day’s entire legislative agenda had been deferred under an agreement. The deputy speaker deferred the entire 58-point agenda, which included 20 private members’ bills. The House, however, took up the two calling attention notices — one related to the high fees and charges being collected by private medical colleges and the other regarding persistent river erosion in Layyah district — besides unanimously passing a resolution to mark Eid Miladun Nabi. The speeches of the opposition members were completely blacked out on the official social media accounts of the National Assembly. Injustice to Sindh Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan and PPP legislators mostly criticised the federal government over long and frequent power outages in Karachi and other parts of Sindh. Another PPP MNA Sharmila Faruqui highlighted the alleged contradiction in the federal government’s development priorities, stating that while “the government repeatedly cites lack of fiscal space, it has approved Rs49bn in federal financing for the first phase of Lahore-Sahiwal-Bahawalnagar Motorway.” On the other hand, she said, the government had released only Rs30bn for the long-delayed strategic Hyderabad-Sukkur Motor­way, terming it a great injustice to the Sindh province. Highlighting some recent incidents, including the murder of Hina Javed in Rawalpindi, some lawmakers expressed serious concerns over the increase in violence against women in the country. Babar Nawaz and Shaista Khan of the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) referring to the murder of five-year-old Ayat Noor in Haripur, lashed out at the PTI-led provincial government, questioning the alleged silence of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and other party MPAs over the incident. The MNAs asked the KP government to take notice of the incident and bring the culprits to justice. New provinces PPP lawmaker Agha Rafiullah demanded that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif should come to the House to give a policy statement on the issue of new provinces. Referring to a statement by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, the PPP MNA from Karachi alleged that a cabinet member had charge-sheeted his own government by declaring that the system had collapsed in the country. On the other hand, PML-N lawmaker Babar Nawaz said the people of Hazara didn’t want to live under the present set-up and they wanted to have a separate province.
